issues.explanation: Gunshot noise is difficult to reconcile as a primary trauma-linked trigger for childhood physical abuse by a caregiver, especially when no other items suggest weapon-related or combat/shooting associations.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin
issues.explanation: A highly specific temperature-on-skin trigger is not impossible, but with the rest of the profile it lacks a plausible link to the stated trauma and is unsupported by memory or threat content; together with gunshot noise it makes the trigger set feel clinically disconnected from caregiver physical abuse.

issues.item: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: For childhood physical abuse by a caregiver, the profile is otherwise organized around shame/self-concept and social avoidance. 'Body Unreliable' is less coherent with the rest of the selected items because there are no accompanying threat or memory items indicating prominent somatic threat, dissociation, injury-related beliefs, or body-based trauma processing. Within this formulation, Negative Appraisals is strongly linked to maladaptive avoidance and modestly linked with triggers; the other appraisals fit that pattern, but this item introduces a distinct body-failure theme that is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

vignette:
Rajesh

Rajesh was thirty-six when he first walked into the precinct after a decade as a detective, but something fundamental had already begun to fracture in him long before that—something that traced back to a childhood he had spent years trying to outrun. His father had been a man of sudden rages and harder hands, someone whose moods could shift with a door slamming or the particular quality of silence that fell when everyone in the house was waiting for the next blow. Rajesh had learned early to read the room, to anticipate, to flinch before contact. By the time he was ten, he had internalized a simple, terrible logic: that his father's violence was a response to something defective in him—a weakness, a failure to be the kind of son who could prevent such things. That belief had never really left him, even after his father died and Rajesh built a life that looked, from the outside, like success.

The trauma had crystallized around a particular winter evening when Rajesh was nine. His father had come home in one of his states, and what started as a verbal tirade escalated into a beating that left Rajesh with bruises across his ribs and shoulders, his skin burning with the specific heat of his father's rage transferred through open palms and a leather belt. The cold that followed—his father's sudden withdrawal into icy silence, the house itself seeming to hold its breath—had become, in Rajesh's nervous system, a harbinger of violence. Even now, when he felt certain temperatures against his skin—a particular kind of cold that reminded him of winter, or the sharp heat of fabric against his arm—his body would flood with dread, and with it, a cascade of old certainties: that he was defective, that he could not cope with what his own mind was doing to him. Each time the precinct's ancient heating system kicked in and a draft moved across his desk, or when a colleague brushed past him in the hallway, the thought arrived with the sensation itself: this is proof that you're broken, that you can't handle what your own body is telling you. The triggers had become a language his mind spoke fluently—one that always translated into the same verdict about himself.

Rajesh had managed well enough through his twenties, channeling his hypervigilance into police work, where his ability to read danger and anticipate threat was not a symptom but a skill. He had married Priya five years ago, a woman patient and intelligent, who had tried to understand the walls he kept around himself. But in the past eighteen months, something had broken open. It started with small things—he began staying up later and later, convincing himself that sleep was a vulnerability, that if he remained conscious and alert, he could prevent the disasters his mind kept conjuring. When Priya would suggest they turn in together, or when his work required him to sleep in an unfamiliar place—a stakeout, a conference in another city—panic would seize him. The thought of being alone in the dark, of being defenseless in sleep, was intolerable. He had come to believe that his inability to manage these situations, his need to stay awake, his refusal to be vulnerable even in his own bed, proved what he had always suspected: that he was a lousy coper, that something fundamental was broken in him as a person.

This belief had begun to reshape his life in ways he could no longer hide. When a door would slam at the precinct—a colleague closing a file cabinet too hard, someone pushing through the bullpen door—Rajesh's entire body would seize. In those moments, the interpretation crystallized: This is what you are. This is how broken you are. His conviction that something fundamental was wrong with him meant that ordinary workplace sounds—a phone ringing, footsteps approaching his desk, the squeak of a chair—now snagged his attention and held it, each one a small confirmation of his fragility. His heart would race, his hands would shake, and in those moments, the interpretation crystallized: This is what you are. This is how broken you are. The shame of his reaction, the certainty that he was defective, drove him to avoid the precinct more often. If he had concluded that he was a lousy coper, that something in him was irreparably broken, then staying home wasn't avoidance—it was the only rational response to what he now knew about himself. The belief that he couldn't manage the unpredictability of the precinct, that his hypervigilance and panic were proof of his inadequacy, made isolation feel like the only honest choice. He took personal days, worked from home when he could, and when he did have to come in, he positioned himself near exits and kept his headphones in, trying to create a buffer between himself and the unpredictable sounds of the workplace. Priya had stopped asking him to go out to dinner, to visit friends, to do the ordinary things married people did together. He had told her he was working a difficult case, but the truth was simpler and more devastating: being around people felt dangerous. Their unpredictability, the possibility of sudden noise or unexpected touch, the risk that someone might see him flinch or notice his vigilance—it all felt like exposure of something he could not bear to have witnessed.

The avoidance had metastasized. He stayed up until two, three in the morning, scrolling through his phone, doing anything to delay the moment when sleep would claim him and leave him defenseless. The sleep deprivation, the isolation, the careful avoidance of situations that might trigger his panic—all of it created new circumstances that demanded his vigilance. By staying awake, by keeping himself small and contained, he had inadvertently multiplied the triggers: the exhaustion itself became a state in which any sound felt threatening, any moment of vulnerability felt catastrophic, and the precinct—with its unpredictable sounds and the eyes of colleagues who might notice his deterioration—became a place he could no longer reliably enter. He avoided going out, avoided people, avoided the situations that might trigger the cascade of sensations and shame. But each time he stayed home instead of showing up, each time he chose isolation over connection, the old belief grew stronger: I am not capable. I am not myself anymore. There is something wrong with me. The avoidance itself had become evidence—each day he worked from home, each dinner he declined, each morning he found a reason not to go to the precinct told him something he couldn't easily argue with: that he must be more fragile than other people, or he would have been able to do these things by now. His safety behaviors had drawn a map of his defectiveness around him. The very strategies he had adopted to protect himself had become evidence, in his mind, of his fundamental inadequacy. Rajesh had finally made an appointment with a therapist last month, after Priya found him at three in the morning sitting in the dark of their bedroom, unable to explain why he could not come to bed beside her. What frightened him most was not the memories themselves, but the possibility that she would eventually see him as he saw himself—as someone irreparably damaged, someone who had lost the person he used to be.

violations.explanation: Triggers (cold sensations, door slamming, workplace sounds) and Negative Appraisals (defectiveness, being 'broken') appear throughout but no paragraph explicitly conveys that triggering stimuli causally lead to negative appraisals—the appraisals are presented as pre-existing beliefs rather than triggered responses.

Negative Appraisals (belief in defectiveness) and Maladaptive Strategies (avoidance, sleep deprivation, isolation) co-occur but lack explicit causal language showing that the appraisals drive the strategies; the relationship is implied but not clearly stated within any single paragraph.

Negative Appraisals (self-blame, shame, feeling broken) and Triggers (door slamming, workplace situations) appear separately but no paragraph conveys that negative appraisals causally influence or amplify triggers.

Maladaptive Strategies (avoidance, staying home, isolation) and Negative Appraisals (belief in inadequacy, defectiveness) are described sequentially but lack explicit causal language showing that the avoidance behaviors reinforce or drive the negative beliefs.

Maladaptive Strategies (avoidance, isolation, sleep deprivation) and Triggers (workplace, social situations, sleep) appear throughout but no paragraph explicitly shows that the avoidance behaviors causally lead to encountering or creating triggers.
